hints: Focus on who oxidises whom in Group 17, remembering that oxidising power decreases down the group.
Recall the three distinct colours for the silver halide precipitates, white for chloride, cream for bromide and yellow for iodide.
Consider what happens when hydrogen burns in chlorine and what colour the hydrogen chloride gas formed actually is.
walkthrough:
**Test the bromine and iodide idea**

Think of displacement as a competition for electrons. The more powerful oxidiser higher up the group takes electrons from the ion below it.

$$\text{Br}_2 + 2\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^- + \text{I}_2$$

**Recall the silver nitrate test colours**

This is a classic identification test you must learn by heart. The precipitate colour tells you which halide was present.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{X}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgX}(s)$$
$\text{AgCl}$ is white, $\text{AgBr}$ is cream, $\text{AgI}$ is yellow.

**Check the hydrogen and chlorine reaction**

Hydrogen burns in chlorine with a pale flame to make hydrogen chloride. Both hydrogen and chlorine are coloured or colourless gases, but the product is a sharp, colourless gas.

$$\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}(g)$$

options.A: Incorrect. Bromine is above iodine in Group 17 so it is the stronger oxidising agent. It oxidises $\text{I}^-$ to $\text{I}_2$, it does not reduce $\text{KI}$. The word reduce is the wrong way round.
options.B: Incorrect. Iodide ions with $\text{AgNO}_3$ give silver iodide, $\text{AgI}$, which is a yellow precipitate, not white. White is the colour for chloride.
options.C: Incorrect. Bromide ions with $\text{AgNO}_3$ give silver bromide, $\text{AgBr}$, which is a cream or off-white precipitate, not pure white. Students often confuse white and cream.
options.D: Correct. Chlorine reacts with hydrogen to form hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, which is a colourless gas. This matches the observed reaction $\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}$.
